Main problem

Some areas of our school in Barranquilla get hot enough to make students uncomfortable, especially during breaks and lunchtime. The cafeteria is where students spend those moments, although our data show that the Red Terrace is the hottest space.

We measured the temperature in three school spaces: the Red Terrace, the Cafeteria and the First-Floor Restrooms. We investigated whether sunlight, shade, and the materials used in each space could help explain the temperature differences.

Objective

We aim to compare temperatures in three school areas. We will test whether shade keeps the cafeteria tiles cooler.

What our data say

We took 12 temperature measurements (°C) in each space. These are the key results (the numbers are calculated live from the data in the tool below).

About our measurements: each value is one temperature reading in °C taken in that space. The differences between the cafeteria and the restrooms are small compared with the variation inside each space, while the Red Terrace stands out as clearly hotter and more variable. The tile surface temperatures in the sun and under the shade would be measured separately in the pilot test.

Our measurements are already loaded. You can change any value or name (one value per line; a point or a comma works as the decimal separator) and click Calculate. Leave a box empty to ignore that group.

Measures of central tendency

What do they mean?

Mean: add all values and divide by n. Median: the middle value of the sorted data (if n is even, the average of the two middle values). Mode: the value that appears most often (if no value repeats, there is no mode).

Measures of dispersion

What do they mean?

Range: max − min. Variance (sample): Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1). Standard deviation: √variance. Coefficient of variation: standard deviation ÷ mean × 100%. Interquartile range: Q3 − Q1 (quartiles calculated like Excel's QUARTILE.INC).

Frequency tables

x = class mark · f = absolute frequency · fr = f ÷ n · F = cumulative frequency · Fr = F ÷ n. Each class includes its lower limit and excludes its upper limit: [a, b).

Automatic conclusions

    Proposed solution & our mission

    Solution

    We propose installing a removable shade sail over a section of the cafeteria that receives direct sunlight. To test its effect, we will measure the surface temperature of similar tiles in the sun and under the shade at the same time. This will help us determine whether the shade keeps the tiles cooler.

    Our mission

    Our mission is to make shared spaces at our school more comfortable, especially during breaks and lunchtime. By measuring temperatures and testing practical solutions, we aim to help our school decide where adding shade could make the biggest difference.

    Why start in the cafeteria? In our data the Red Terrace is the hottest and most variable space, but the cafeteria is where students spend their breaks and lunchtime. We start the pilot there, and the Red Terrace is a strong candidate for the next shade sail.

    Examples on other campuses

    Why this solution?

    We chose a removable shade sail because it blocks direct sunlight before it reaches the cafeteria tiles, helping them absorb less heat. We can test its effect by measuring shaded and unshaded tiles at the same time. If the results show a meaningful difference, other schools could try the same approach in their outdoor spaces.

    How we would test it

    We would measure shaded and sun-exposed tiles at the same time over several days. If the shaded tiles consistently stay cooler, the school could extend the design to other outdoor areas.

    Limitations

    • A shade sail only covers part of the cafeteria.
    • The shaded area shifts as the sun moves.
    • The sail may need to be taken down in strong winds.
    • Our test would measure tile temperatures, so we would need separate measurements to find out whether the air also gets cooler.

    Our data also have limits

    We have 12 measurements per space (a sample), so we used sample variance and standard deviation (dividing by n − 1). More days of measurements would make the comparison stronger.

    Next steps

    Choose a test spot

    Check where direct sunlight hits the cafeteria tiles during lunchtime.

    Set up a small pilot

    Install a removable shade sail over one sun-exposed section.

    Measure and compare

    Record the surface temperatures of similar shaded and sun-exposed tiles at the same time over several days.

    Decide whether to expand

    If the shaded tiles consistently stay cooler, use the results to propose where else the school could add shade.

    Our process

    We used an AI assistant (Claude in Excel) to organize our data, calculate the measures with Excel formulas, build the frequency tables and graphs, and create this website. Our main steps were:

    1. Calculate the measures of central tendency and dispersion from a photo of our data.
    2. Present everything in English, including histograms, frequency polygon, ogive and pictogram.
    3. Explain the whole work step by step in Spanish.
    4. Write a log of the process for our teacher.
    5. Prepare website content and an interactive statistics tool.
    6. Apply the Cool Spaces design guide (colors, fonts and content) to the website.
